30-day gesture drawing routine: 10 minutes a day, one thing at a time

A common reason gesture drawing stalls is not skill but trying to see everything at once. This routine gives you one thing to observe each day. Time, pose count and pose type are already chosen, so tap "Start" in the table and draw.

Written and maintained by: Jeremy

Updated November 10, 2026

Before you start

All you need is a pencil and paper you will not mind using up, such as copy paper or a sketchbook. If you draw on a tablet, decide in advance not to use the eraser. Not erasing makes the next line come faster.

  1. Find today's row and tap "Start". The studio opens with those settings.
  2. Draw with only "Observe today" in mind. Everything else is allowed to be wrong.
  3. When you finish, photograph the pages together and answer "Check yourself" in one line.

If you miss a day, just move on. Thirty days is an order, not a deadline. After three days off, pick up from the next day.

Week 1: one line for the big flow (30 seconds)

Week 1 is only about the line of action: one line that sums up where the whole pose is heading and how its force flows. It often runs close to the spine but is not a tracing of it, and it usually travels from the head toward the foot carrying the most weight. Keep its shape simple: a C curve, an S curve, or a straight line.

DaySettingObserve todayCheck yourselfStart
130 sec × 10 poses · All posesMark two dots, top of the head and the feet, then join them with one lineCan you read the pose without hands or a face?Start
230 sec × 10 poses · Standing & weight shiftOne line from the head, through the pelvis, down to the foot on the floorDid the line come down toward the weight-bearing foot rather than between the feet?Start
330 sec × 10 poses · Walking & runningHow far the torso leans forwardDid an upright torso make the figure look like it stopped walking?Start
430 sec × 10 poses · Reaching, bending & twistingTell a C curve from an S curveDid you bend it the opposite way from the photo?Start
530 sec × 15 poses · Jumping, sport & danceExaggerate the curve slightly beyond the photoDoes the movement read better with the exaggeration?Start
61 min × 5 poses · All posesPlace three masses on the line: head, rib cage, pelvisIs the first flow still alive after adding the masses?Start
730 sec × 10 poses · All posesReview: pick the clearest and the least clear drawing from the weekIs the difference the number of lines, or their direction?Start

For more detail, read 30-second line of action: one line for a walking figure.

Week 2: where is the weight? (1 minute)

In week 2 the poses get one minute, and you look at tilts and balance. When a standing figure looks wrong, the cause is often where the weight sits, not the size of the head.

DaySettingObserve todayCheck yourselfStart
81 min × 10 poses · Standing & weight shiftCompare the angle of the shoulder line and the hip lineDid you draw the two lines parallel out of habit?Start
91 min × 10 poses · Standing & weight shiftDrop an imaginary vertical line from the middle of the torso to the floorDoes it land toward the supporting foot, or between the feet if the weight is shared?Start
101 min × 10 poses · Pushing, pulling & liftingThe direction of effort and the direction the body leansIs the body standing straight while pulling something heavy?Start
111 min × 10 poses · Walking & runningDraw the planted leg darker and the lifted leg lighterCan you tell which foot is down from line weight alone?Start
121 min × 10 poses · Daily life & toolsWhich way the weight of a bag, umbrella or cup pulls the bodyWithout the object, does the figure still look like it is holding something?Start
131 min × 10 poses · Emotion & communicationRead emotion from the shoulders and chest, not the faceDoes the emotion come through with the face covered?Start
1430 sec × 5 poses · All poses, then 1 min × 5 poses · All posesReview: put week 1's flow and week 2's tilts into the same drawingDo the 30-second drawings include the shoulder and hip tilts too?Start

1-minute balance: read the pelvis and supporting foot together walks through the same observation on one photo.

Week 3: masses and overlaps (3 minutes)

Week 3 uses three-minute poses. Longer time tempts you to trace outlines; this week, do the opposite and see the body as boxes and cylinders, and notice what sits in front.

DaySettingObserve todayCheck yourselfStart
153 min × 5 poses · Chair & seat posesWhere the pelvis meets the seat, and how short a thigh looks when it points toward youDid you draw the thigh at its standing length?Start
163 min × 5 poses · Floor, kneeling & crouchingKeep the outline of the front leg unbroken where the legs overlapDoes the back leg's line cut across the front leg?Start
173 min × 5 poses · Lying & recliningStart with the pelvis and shoulders touching the floor, not the headDoes the body rest its weight on the floor instead of floating?Start
183 min × 5 poses · Reaching, bending & twistingDraw the rib cage and pelvis as boxes facing different waysAre both boxes facing the same way?Start
193 min × 5 poses · Jumping, sport & danceUse the head length as a ruler for the arms and legsDid you compare how many heads long the reaching arm is?Start
203 min × 5 poses · All posesSimplify hands to mittens and feet to wedgesDid time run out while you were drawing fingers?Start
211 min × 10 poses · All posesReview: fit the three-minute masses into one minuteCan you see the rib cage and pelvis directions in one-minute drawings?Start

For seated poses, read 3-minute seated pose: find the pelvis and read overlaps alongside this week.

Week 4: mix, flip, and use your own photos

The last week applies everything under new conditions. The same structure looks new when the time or direction changes.

DaySettingObserve todayCheck yourselfStart
2230 sec × 10 poses · Standing & weight shift, then 3 min × 3 poses · Standing & weight shiftDraw the same type short and many, then long and few, and compareDid the three-minute drawings lose the flow the 30-second ones had?Start
231 min × 10 poses · All posesSwitch the level to advanced; spend the first 10 seconds on the line of action onlyThe harder the pose, did the big flow still come first?Start
2445 sec × 15 poses · All posesChange your rhythm with an unfamiliar timeWith an awkward time limit, what did you drop first?Start
253 min × 5 poses · My photos tabDraw from photos of family, friends, or yourself in a mirrorCompared with the prepared poses, what was harder?Start
261 min × 10 poses · All posesAfter each pose, flip it and draw it againDid flipping reveal tilt mistakes in your drawing?Start
273 min × 5 poses · Emotion & communicationGive each pose one line of dialogue and draw so it showsCan you imagine the scene with the dialogue hidden?Start
281 min × 10 poses · All posesReview: lay out four weeks of drawings in date orderWhat changed most: lines, proportions, or tilts?Start

For day 25, choose photos in the studio's "My photos" tab. They are never uploaded and stay on your device. For day 26, use the "Mirror" button or the M key in the practice screen.

Days 29–30: put day 1 beside today

DaySettingObserve todayStart
2930 sec × 10 poses · All posesDraw again with exactly the day 1 settings. On the review screen that follows, use "One thing to watch next time" to choose your weakest area: line of action, balance, or overlap and proportion.Start
30—A day without drawing. Put the day 1 and day 29 drawings side by side, copy the table below onto paper, and fill it in. The goal you chose appears again in the studio's practice log.—
CheckDay 1Day 29
What did you draw first?
Did head to feet fit on the page?
Can you see which foot carries the weight?
Did you run out of time on each pose?

When you compare, look at what you now notice first, not at how good the drawing is. If day 1 started with the face and day 29 started with the line of action, the routine has done its job.

After 30 days

  • Run the routine again with week 1 at one minute and week 3 at five minutes.
  • Or repeat only your weakest week for another seven days.
  • If you are not sure where to begin, start with A 10-minute figure drawing routine for beginners.
  • If the same problem keeps coming back, look it up in seven reasons gesture drawings look off.

The observation methods here gather widely taught material from the sources below into a practice sequence. Checked on November 10, 2026.

  • Balance line and supporting foot: How to Draw Balanced Poses (Proko)
  • Simplifying rib cage and pelvis as boxes: How to Draw Structure in the Body – Robo Bean (Proko)
  • Measuring proportion in head lengths: Body proportions (Wikipedia), Measuring Techniques (Proko)
  • Foreshortening: Foreshortening (Wikipedia)
